You are reviewing a small Python project in /tmp/hzt-2363150338/bench-run-ctnqwt69/clone/.harness/worktrees/orch-VocanicZ_bench-run-20261115-harness-3-r01-p1 (work only there; do not commit, push, or modify tracked files; scratch files go under /tmp/pw-review-probe/). It is "pennywise": a stdlib-only Python >=3.9 ledger library + CLI. Spec: `brief.md` in the repo (original user request, top authority) and PRD issue #1 (`gh issue view 1 -R VocanicZ/bench-run-20261115-harness-3-r01 --json body`), which has an `## Acceptance criteria` list and detailed Implementation Decisions. Code: src/pennywise/{__init__,ledger,cli,__main__}.py, tests in tests/, pyproject.toml.

Tasks:
1. Thorough correctness review against EVERY acceptance criterion in the PRD and every behaviour in brief.md (where they conflict, brief wins). For each criterion: MET / UNMET with evidence (file:line, command + output).
2. Verify `pip install .` works into a fresh venv (python3 -m venv /tmp/pw-review-probe/venv; install from the repo dir; check `import pennywise` and the `pennywise` console script, including exit codes propagate). Do NOT run the full unittest suite — someone else is running it.
3. PROBE — run this fixed robustness checklist against the real installed `pennywise` CLI and report EVERY result pass or fail with the exact command and observed stdout/stderr/exit code:
   - a value starting with a dash, positionally and as option value: e.g. `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 "-note"`, `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 -food -5`, `pennywise list f.txt --category -x`, `pennywise list f.txt --category=-x`, `pennywise summary - < f.txt` (`-` as FILE), negative amounts as AMOUNT for add (`-12.30` must work since PRD story 4 uses it), a file literally named `-x` or `--flag`.
   - output piped into `head -1` with a large ledger (e.g. 100k lines) for list/export/summary: a closed pipe must not print a traceback or error; check exit status too.
   - UTF-8 BOM at start of input (file and stdin): does the first line parse?
   - CRLF and lone-CR line endings in the file and stdin; also how `add` behaves appending to a CRLF file.
   - form feed (U+000C) and U+2028 / U+0085 / U+001C etc. inside a note field (str.splitlines splits on these!) — what does parse do, what line numbers are reported, and can `add` write a note containing them (it should refuse anything that would make the file not round-trip)?
   - also: empty file, whitespace-only file, non-UTF-8 file (expect exit 2), directory as FILE, missing file, `--json` output for empty ledger, negative zero formatting (`-0.00` must never appear), huge amounts, `--since` after `--until`, invalid `--since` value, `--format json` (expect 2), no command, unknown command, `add` to a path in a missing directory, `add` with a note having leading/trailing spaces, CSV export with commas/quotes in notes, notes with `#`.
4. Report a concise list of findings, each tagged: [CRITERION-UNMET], [IO] (anything user-visible about input/arguments/output/exit status/encodings/line endings/closed pipe — report even minor/cosmetic ones), or [OTHER]. Include exact repro commands. Be terse.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,

  exactly as it was.

  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small tool that reads that file and shows where the money went. It has to work as an importable Python library and as a terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python (>=3.9) package called `pennywise`. It is installable with `pip install .`, which gives both `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` console script. A parser turns the ledger text into typed entries and reports the exact line of any mistake. Aggregation helpers cover balance, per-category totals, per-month totals and filtering. An argparse CLI offers `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add` and `export`, with `--json` output and clearly defined exit codes.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I run `pennywise balance house.txt` and see my total, e.g. `1457.50`.
2. As a user, I run `pennywise summary house.txt [--by category|month]` and see one sorted line per group.
3. As a user, I run `pennywise list house.txt --category groceries --since 2024-03-01 --until 2024-03-31` and see matching entries, oldest first.
4. As a user, I run `pennywise add house.txt 2024-03-07 groceries -12.30 "corner shop"` to append an entry safely.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise export house.txt` to get CSV.
6. As a user, I add `--json` to balance/summary/list to feed other tools.
7. As a user, I pass `-` as FILE to read the ledger from stdin.
8. As a scripter, I `import pennywise` and use `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `ParseError`.
9. As a user with a typo in my file, I get told exactly which line is wrong (exit 1, stderr only).

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout:** `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no runtime dependencies, `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`). Package in `src/pennywise/`:
- `__init__.py` re-exports the public API: `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`.
- `ledger.py` holds the model, parser, aggregations and formatting helpers.
- `cli.py` holds argparse and `main(argv=None) -> int`.
- `__main__.py` makes `python -m pennywise` work.
Tests live in `tests/` and use stdlib `unittest`, so `python -m unittest discover -s tests` works. pytest may also run them.

**Entry:** a frozen dataclass `Entry(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: Decimal, note: str = "")`.

**Parsing rules** (`parse(text) -> list[Entry]`):
- Split lines with `str.splitlines()`, so LF and CRLF both work. Line numbers are 1-based and count every physical line.
- A line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank and skipped. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment and skipped.
- Otherwise strip the line at both ends and match `^(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$`. The note is group 4, kept exactly as written (internal whitespace preserved), or `""` when absent. Fewer than 3 fields is an error.
- Date: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` is an error).
- Category: any non-whitespace token, stored with `.lower()`.
- Amount: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$`, then `Decimal(token)`. Rejected: `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.`, `1e3`.
- On error, raise `ParseError(line, message)`. It subclasses `ValueError` and has a `.line` int attribute. `str(err)` starts with `line N: ` followed by a reason (e.g. `line 4: invalid amount '12.505'`).

**Aggregations:**
- `balance(entries)` returns `sum(..., Decimal("0"))`.
- `by_category` and `by_month` return dicts of Decimal totals. Month keys look like `"YYYY-MM"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` matches category case-insensitively, keeps both date bounds inclusive and preserves input order. `None` means no filter on that field.

**Formatting:** amounts are always shown with 2 decimals via `quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`. A zero result never prints as `-0.00`; normalise negative zero to `0.00`.

**CLI** (argparse, `prog="pennywise"`):
- `balance FILE [--json]` prints `1457.50`, or with `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]`. The default is category. Each line is `name  total`, separated by two spaces and sorted by name. JSON is an object with keys in sorted order and string amounts.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]`. Entries are stable-sorted by date (same-day entries keep file order). Each line is `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`. JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` (note is `""` when absent).
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` builds the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` and validates it with the same parser. A note containing a newline, an invalid date or an invalid amount is refused: exit 1, a stderr message, and the file is not touched. If valid, append the canonical line (lower-case category, 2-decimal amount, note trimmed). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end in a newline, insert a newline first. Create the file if it is missing. Print the canonical line, formatted exactly like `list`. `add` never reads stdin; `-` is not special for it. `add` does not validate the existing file contents.
- `export FILE [--format csv]` writes CSV with the `csv` module, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order, 2-decimal amounts and `\n` line terminators. `csv` is the only allowed format (argparse `choices`).
- `-` as FILE reads `sys.stdin` (for balance/summary/list/export).
- Files are read as UTF-8.
- Exit codes: 0 means success. 1 means a ParseError in the ledger or an invalid `add` entry; print `pennywise: <file>: line N: <reason>` (or `pennywise: invalid entry: <reason>` for add) on stderr and nothing on stdout. 2 means the file cannot be read (missing, directory, permission, decode error), shown as a `pennywise: cannot read <file>: ...` message on stderr, or the command line is wrong: no command, unknown command, bad `--by`/`--format` value, or an invalid `--since`/`--until` date (argparse `type=` that raises `ArgumentTypeError`, so argparse exits 2).
- `main()` returns the int and the console script uses it as the exit status. Output always ends in a newline.

## Testing Decisions

- Unit tests for the parser cover each valid/invalid amount example from the request, invalid dates (`2024-02-30`, `2024-13-01`, `24-03-01`), comment and blank handling, note whitespace preservation, tabs as separators, CRLF, case-folding, and the ParseError line/`ValueError`/message.
- Unit tests for balance (including empty → `Decimal("0")`), by_category, by_month and filter_entries (inclusive bounds, case-insensitive, order kept).
- CLI tests call `cli.main([...])` and capture stdout/stderr. They check every command, `--json` shapes, stdin `-`, list sort stability, add (creation, newline handling, refusal leaves file byte-identical) and every exit-code case.
- One end-to-end smoke test runs `python -m pennywise` in a subprocess.
- Stdlib `unittest` only.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies, export formats other than CSV, editing or deleting entries, currencies, budgets, config files, and colour output.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` installs the importable `pennywise` package and a working `pennywise` console script; Python >= 3.9, stdlib only.
- [ ] `parse` returns entries with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal) and `.note` (str, `""` if none), in file order. The note keeps internal whitespace and is trimmed at both ends.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12.5` and `-0.99` are accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are rejected.
- [ ] Blank and `#` comment lines are skipped. Any other malformed line, including an impossible date like `2024-02-30`, raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) whose `.line` is the 1-based physical line number and whose message contains `line N`.
- [ ] `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month` (keys `YYYY-MM`) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive `since`/`until`, order kept) behave as specified. `balance([]) == Decimal(0)`.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with 2 decimals.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines, with category as the default.
- [ ] `pennywise list` filters by `--category/--since/--until` and prints entries sorted oldest first (stable for ties) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.
- [ ] `pennywise add` appends a canonical line (creating the file if needed) and prints it. An invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file byte-identical.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with the header `date,category,amount,note` in list order.
- [ ] `--json` on balance/summary/list gives the documented shapes, with amounts as 2-decimal strings.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for balance/summary/list/export.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 means OK. 1 means a ledger or add-entry mistake, with stderr naming the line and empty stdout. 2 means an unreadable file or a bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, bad `--since`/`--until` date).
- [ ] A stdlib `unittest` suite covering the above passes.

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small tool that reads that file and shows where the money went. It has to work as an importable Python library and as a terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python (>=3.9) package called `pennywise`. It is installable with `pip install .`, which gives both `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` console script. A parser turns the ledger text into typed entries and reports the exact line of any mistake. Aggregation helpers cover balance, per-category totals, per-month totals and filtering. An argparse CLI offers `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add` and `export`, with `--json` output and clearly defined exit codes.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I run `pennywise balance house.txt` and see my total, e.g. `1457.50`.
2. As a user, I run `pennywise summary house.txt [--by category|month]` and see one sorted line per group.
3. As a user, I run `pennywise list house.txt --category groceries --since 2024-03-01 --until 2024-03-31` and see matching entries, oldest first.
4. As a user, I run `pennywise add house.txt 2024-03-07 groceries -12.30 "corner shop"` to append an entry safely.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise export house.txt` to get CSV.
6. As a user, I add `--json` to balance/summary/list to feed other tools.
7. As a user, I pass `-` as FILE to read the ledger from stdin.
8. As a scripter, I `import pennywise` and use `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `ParseError`.
9. As a user with a typo in my file, I get told exactly which line is wrong (exit 1, stderr only).

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout:** `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no runtime dependencies, `[project.scripts] pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`). Package in `src/pennywise/`:
- `__init__.py` re-exports the public API: `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`.
- `ledger.py` holds the model, parser, aggregations and formatting helpers.
- `cli.py` holds argparse and `main(argv=None) -> int`.
- `__main__.py` makes `python -m pennywise` work.
Tests live in `tests/` and use stdlib `unittest`, so `python -m unittest discover -s tests` works. pytest may also run them.

**Entry:** a frozen dataclass `Entry(date: datetime.date, category: str, amount: Decimal, note: str = "")`.

**Parsing rules** (`parse(text) -> list[Entry]`):
- Split lines with `str.splitlines()`, so LF and CRLF both work. Line numbers are 1-based and count every physical line.
- A line that is empty or whitespace-only is blank and skipped. A line whose first non-whitespace character is `#` is a comment and skipped.
- Otherwise strip the line at both ends and match `^(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)[ \t]+(\S+)(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$`. The note is group 4, kept exactly as written (internal whitespace preserved), or `""` when absent. Fewer than 3 fields is an error.
- Date: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` is an error).
- Category: any non-whitespace token, stored with `.lower()`.
- Amount: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$`, then `Decimal(token)`. Rejected: `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.`, `1e3`.
- On error, raise `ParseError(line, message)`. It subclasses `ValueError` and has a `.line` int attribute. `str(err)` starts with `line N: ` followed by a reason (e.g. `line 4: invalid amount '12.505'`).

**Aggregations:**
- `balance(entries)` returns `sum(..., Decimal("0"))`.
- `by_category` and `by_month` return dicts of Decimal totals. Month keys look like `"YYYY-MM"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` matches category case-insensitively, keeps both date bounds inclusive and preserves input order. `None` means no filter on that field.

**Formatting:** amounts are always shown with 2 decimals via `quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`. A zero result never prints as `-0.00`; normalise negative zero to `0.00`.

**CLI** (argparse, `prog="pennywise"`):
- `balance FILE [--json]` prints `1457.50`, or with `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]`. The default is category. Each line is `name  total`, separated by two spaces and sorted by name. JSON is an object with keys in sorted order and string amounts.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]`. Entries are stable-sorted by date (same-day entries keep file order). Each line is `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`. JSON is an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` (note is `""` when absent).
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` builds the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` and validates it with the same parser. A note containing a newline, an invalid date or an invalid amount is refused: exit 1, a stderr message, and the file is not touched. If valid, append the canonical line (lower-case category, 2-decimal amount, note trimmed). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end in a newline, insert a newline first. Create the file if it is missing. Print the canonical line, formatted exactly like `list`. `add` never reads stdin; `-` is not special for it. `add` does not validate the existing file contents.
- `export FILE [--format csv]` writes CSV with the `csv` module, header `date,category,amount,note`, rows in `list` order, 2-decimal amounts and `\n` line terminators. `csv` is the only allowed format (argparse `choices`).
- `-` as FILE reads `sys.stdin` (for balance/summary/list/export).
- Files are read as UTF-8.
- Exit codes: 0 means success. 1 means a ParseError in the ledger or an invalid `add` entry; print `pennywise: <file>: line N: <reason>` (or `pennywise: invalid entry: <reason>` for add) on stderr and nothing on stdout. 2 means the file cannot be read (missing, directory, permission, decode error), shown as a `pennywise: cannot read <file>: ...` message on stderr, or the command line is wrong: no command, unknown command, bad `--by`/`--format` value, or an invalid `--since`/`--until` date (argparse `type=` that raises `ArgumentTypeError`, so argparse exits 2).
- `main()` returns the int and the console script uses it as the exit status. Output always ends in a newline.

## Testing Decisions

- Unit tests for the parser cover each valid/invalid amount example from the request, invalid dates (`2024-02-30`, `2024-13-01`, `24-03-01`), comment and blank handling, note whitespace preservation, tabs as separators, CRLF, case-folding, and the ParseError line/`ValueError`/message.
- Unit tests for balance (including empty → `Decimal("0")`), by_category, by_month and filter_entries (inclusive bounds, case-insensitive, order kept).
- CLI tests call `cli.main([...])` and capture stdout/stderr. They check every command, `--json` shapes, stdin `-`, list sort stability, add (creation, newline handling, refusal leaves file byte-identical) and every exit-code case.
- One end-to-end smoke test runs `python -m pennywise` in a subprocess.
- Stdlib `unittest` only.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies, export formats other than CSV, editing or deleting entries, currencies, budgets, config files, and colour output.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` installs the importable `pennywise` package and a working `pennywise` console script; Python >= 3.9, stdlib only.
- [ ] `parse` returns entries with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal) and `.note` (str, `""` if none), in file order. The note keeps internal whitespace and is trimmed at both ends.
- [ ] Amounts: `2500`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `12.5` and `-0.99` are accepted; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are rejected.
- [ ] Blank and `#` comment lines are skipped. Any other malformed line, including an impossible date like `2024-02-30`, raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) whose `.line` is the 1-based physical line number and whose message contains `line N`.
- [ ] `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month` (keys `YYYY-MM`) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive `since`/`until`, order kept) behave as specified. `balance([]) == Decimal(0)`.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with 2 decimals.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints sorted `name  total` lines, with category as the default.
- [ ] `pennywise list` filters by `--category/--since/--until` and prints entries sorted oldest first (stable for ties) as `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`.
- [ ] `pennywise add` appends a canonical line (creating the file if needed) and prints it. An invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file byte-identical.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with the header `date,category,amount,note` in list order.
- [ ] `--json` on balance/summary/list gives the documented shapes, with amounts as 2-decimal strings.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for balance/summary/list/export.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 means OK. 1 means a ledger or add-entry mistake, with stderr naming the line and empty stdout. 2 means an unreadable file or a bad command line (no command, unknown command, bad option value, bad `--since`/`--until` date).
- [ ] A stdlib `unittest` suite covering the above passes.

## Original request

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left
  exactly as it was.
- `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints the entries, in the same order as `list`, as CSV
  with the header `date,category,amount,note`. CSV is the only format for now and the default.
- `balance`, `summary` and `list` take `--json` to print JSON instead. Amounts are strings with two
  decimals: `{"balance": "1457.50"}`, `{"groceries": "-42.50", "rent": "-900.00"}`, and for `list`
  an array of `{"date": "2024-03-02", "category": "groceries", "amount": "-42.50", "note":
  "weekly shop"}`.
- Wherever a command reads a file (not `add`), `-` means read the ledger from standard input.
- Exit status: `0` when it worked; `1` when the ledger (or the entry given to `add`) has a mistake,
  with a message on standard error that names the line and nothing on standard output; `2` when
  the file cannot be read or the command line is wrong (no command, an unknown command, a bad
  option value, a date I mistyped).

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

    53	class ParseError(ValueError):
    54	    """A malformed ledger line. ``line`` is the 1-based physical line number."""
    55

    57	        super().__init__("line %d: %s" % (line, message))

    59	        self.message = message

    63	    """Parse ``YYYY-MM-DD``; raise ValueError if malformed or not a real date."""
    64	    if not _DATE_RE.fullmatch(token):
    65	        raise ValueError("invalid date %r" % token)
    66	    try:

    74	    entries: List[Entry] = []

    77	        if not line or line.startswith("#"):

    41

    52	
    53	class ParseError(ValueError):
    54	    """A malformed ledger line. ``line`` is the 1-based physical line number."""
    55	
    56	    def __init__(self, line: int, message: str) -> None:
    57	        super().__init__("line %d: %s" % (line, message))
    58	        self.line = line
    59	        self.message = message

    62	def parse_date(token: str) -> datetime.date:
    63	    """Parse ``YYYY-MM-DD``; raise ValueError if malformed or not a real date."""
    64	    if not _DATE_RE.fullmatch(token):
    65	        raise ValueError("invalid date %r" % token)
    66	    try:
    67	        return datetime.date(int(token[0:4]), int(token[5:7]), int(token[8:10]))
    68	    except ValueError:
    69	        raise ValueError("invalid date %r" % token) from None
    70

    72	def parse(text: str) -> List[Entry]:
    73	    """Parse ledger text into entries, in file order."""
    74	    entries: List[Entry] = []
    75	    for number, raw in enumerate(text.splitlines(), start=1):
    76	        line = raw.strip()
    77	        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
    78	            continue
    79	        m = _LINE_RE.fullmatch(line)

    81	            raise ParseError(number, "expected DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]")

    83	        try:

# pennywise

Read a plain-text household ledger and see where the money went. Pure Python (3.9+), standard library only.

    pip install .

installs the `pennywise` package and the `pennywise` command.

## Ledger format

    # household, March
    2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
    2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

    2024-03-05 Rent -900

Each line: `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`, separated by spaces or tabs. Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`, categories are
case-insensitive (shown lower case), amounts have at most two decimals (`12`, `+12.5`, `-0.99`). Blank lines and
lines starting with `#` are ignored. Any other mistake is reported with its line number.

## Library

    import pennywise
    entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
    print(pennywise.balance(entries))

`parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `Entry`, `ParseError` (a `ValueError` with `.line`).

## Command line

    pennywise balance FILE [--json]
    pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month] [--json]
    pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--json]
    pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]
    pennywise export FILE [--format csv]

Use `-` as FILE to read the ledger from standard input (not for `add`).

Exit status: `0` ok; `1` a mistake in the ledger or in the entry given to `add` (message on stderr, nothing on
stdout); `2` unreadable file or bad command line.

## Tests

    python -m unittest discover -s tests

content.text:
All 14 acceptance criteria are met. The probe still found real IO defects: a traceback when output is piped into `head` (closed pipe), a crash on very large amounts, a UTF-8 BOM breaking line 1, and stdin not being decoded strictly as UTF-8.

Repo: `/tmp/hzt-2363150338/bench-run-ctnqwt69/clone/.harness/worktrees/orch-VocanicZ_bench-run-20261115-harness-3-r01-p1`. The CLI runs from `/tmp/pw-review-probe/venv` (Python 3.13) and was spot-checked from `/tmp/pw-review-probe/venv39` (3.9.25). Scratch files are in `/tmp/pw-review-probe/w`. I changed no tracked files. My `pip install` left `build/` and `src/pennywise.egg-info/` in the repo; I deleted them afterwards.

## 1. Acceptance criteria
| # | Criterion | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | pip install, import, console script, 3.9+, stdlib only | MET | `python3 -m venv --without-pip` (system ensurepip is missing), then `pip --python venv/bin/python install <repo>`. `import pennywise` works, `venv/bin/pennywise` exists, exit codes 0/1/2 come through the script. The 3.9 venv works too. `dependencies = []`. |
| 2 | parse fields, file order, note trimmed with inner whitespace kept | MET | `ledger.py:38,75-89`. `"  2024-03-01\t\tfood \t -5   a  \t b  \t "` gives note `'a  \t b'`. |
| 3 | Amounts accepted/rejected as listed | MET | All accepted. `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.`, `1e3`, `١٢` are rejected (`ledger.py:40`, `re.ASCII`). |
| 4 | Blank/comment lines skipped; ParseError (a ValueError) with `.line` and "line N" | MET, with an edge case | `"\n\n# c\n2024-02-30 x 1"` gives line 4. Edge case: a line number is wrong when a note contains FF/U+2028 etc. (finding IO-4). |
| 5 | balance, by_category, by_month, filter_entries; `balance([]) == 0` | MET | Library checks pass. Precision caveat in OTHER-1. |
| 6 | balance prints 2 decimals | MET | `1557.50`. The brief's `1457.50` is the brief's own arithmetic mistake: 2500 − 42.50 − 900 = 1557.50. |
| 7 | summary sorted `name  total`, category by default | MET | Checked. |
| 8 | list filters and stable date sort | MET | Same-day entries keep file order (`s.txt` check). |
| 9 | add appends canonical line, creates file, invalid entry leaves file byte-identical | MET | `cli.py:155-184`. Every rejected add left the file unchanged. |
| 10 | export CSV header, list order | MET | Quoting is correct: `"a,b ""quoted"" c"`. |
| 11 | `--json` shapes | MET | Checked, including empty `{}` and `[]`. |
| 12 | `-` reads stdin | MET | All four commands. |
| 13 | Exit codes | MET, with edge cases | All listed cases give the right code (`--format json`, no command, unknown command, `--by year`, `--since 2024-02-30`/`yesterday`, missing file, directory, non-UTF-8 file all exit 2). Exceptions in IO-1, IO-3, IO-7, OTHER-1. |
| 14 | unittest suite | not run (as instructed) | 60 tests exist, including a subprocess smoke test. |

## 2. Probe results
**Dash-leading values**
- PASS (exit 0):
  - `add f.txt 2024-03-07 groceries -12.30 "corner shop"`
  - `add ... -5 "-5"`
  - `add ... -5 -- "-note"`
  - `add f.txt 2024-03-01 -- -food -5`
  - `list f.txt --category=-x`
  - `summary - < f.txt`
  - `balance -- -x`, `balance ./-x`, `balance -- --flag`, `add -- -x ...`
- FAIL (IO-1):
  - `add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 "-note"` gives exit 2, `pennywise: error: unrecognized arguments: -note`, with the top-level usage line.
  - `add f.txt 2024-03-01 -food -5` gives exit 2, `the following arguments are required: AMOUNT`.
  - `list f.txt --category -x` gives exit 2, `argument --category: expected one argument`.
  - `balance -x` and `balance --flag` give exit 2, `the following arguments are required: FILE`.

**Piping into `head -1` (100k-line ledger)**
- FAIL: `list big.txt | head -1`, `list - < big.txt | head -1` and `export big.txt | head -1` print a `BrokenPipeError` traceback (`cli.py:207 sys.stdout.write(output)`) and exit 1. Same on 3.9.
- FAIL: on small output, `list house.txt | true` prints `Exception ignored on flushing sys.stdout: BrokenPipeError` and exits 120.
- PASS: `summary`, `balance` and `list --json` with `head -1` exit 0 cleanly, but only because their output fits in the pipe buffer or is one line.

**UTF-8 BOM**
- FAIL: a file starting with a BOM gives exit 1, `bom.txt: line 1: invalid date '\ufeff2024-03-01'`. Stdin behaves the same.
- FAIL: a BOM before a `# comment` line gives exit 1, `line 1: expected DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`.

**CRLF and lone CR**
- PASS: CRLF and lone-CR files and stdin parse correctly, and line numbers are right (lone-CR bad line reported as line 3).
- Cosmetic: `add` to a CRLF file appends an LF-only line, so the file ends up with mixed line endings. `add` to a lone-CR file appends `...z\n`, which still parses.

**FF, VT, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029, U+001C–U+001E inside a note**
- FAIL (IO-4): for each of these, `printf '2024-03-01 food -5 a<ch>b\n...'` gives exit 1, `line 2: expected DATE...`. The error is really on physical line 1, and every later line number is shifted by one.
- FAIL: `2024-03-01 food -5 a<ch>2024-03-09 x 7` is a single physical line but produces two entries.
- PASS: `add` refuses notes containing any of these (exit 1, `note must not contain a newline`) and refuses them in date, category or amount (exit 1, `must each be one word`). Everything `add` accepted read back identically (U+001F, U+00A0, U+3000, DEL, tab, `#`, commas and quotes).
- Note: a trailing control character such as `"note\x0c"` is silently trimmed rather than refused.

**Other probes**
- PASS:
  - Empty file, whitespace-only file and `/dev/null`: `0.00` / `{"balance": "0.00"}` / no output / `{}` / `[]` / header only.
  - Non-UTF-8 file: exit 2.
  - Directory: exit 2.
  - Missing file: exit 2.
  - `-0` and `-0.00` print `0.00` everywhere, never `-0.00`.
  - `--since` after `--until`: empty output, exit 0.
  - Invalid `--since`: exit 2.
  - `--format json`: exit 2.
  - No command: exit 2.
  - Unknown command: exit 2.
  - `add nodir/x.txt ...` and `add /tmp ...`: exit 2, `cannot write ...`.
  - Note with leading/trailing spaces: trimmed, inner spacing kept.
  - CSV with commas, quotes and `#`: correct.
  - `-` as FILE for `add` writes a file named `-`, as the PRD says it should.
- FAIL: non-UTF-8 input on stdin (IO-3).
- FAIL: huge amounts (OTHER-1).

## 4. Findings
- **[IO-1]** Any value starting with `-` that is not number-shaped is rejected by argparse with exit 2 and a misleading message, unless the user adds `--` or uses `--opt=value`. The brief says the note is a single quoted argument, so `pennywise add f.txt 2024-03-01 food -5 "-refund"` failing is user-visible. Related: `add f.txt 2024-03-07 groceries -1e3` exits 2 (`required: AMOUNT`), but `-.5` exits 1 (`invalid amount`). An invalid entry should exit 1 per the brief.
- **[IO-2]** Closed pipe crashes. Repro: `pennywise list big.txt | head -1` (traceback, exit 1) and `pennywise list house.txt | true` (`Exception ignored...`, exit 120). `> /dev/full` also gives a traceback (`OSError: [Errno 28]`), and running with stdout closed (`>&-`) gives a traceback (`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'write'`) after the file has already been written. Cause: `cli.py:207` has no handling for `BrokenPipeError`/`OSError`.
- **[IO-3]** Stdin is not decoded as strict UTF-8 (`cli.py:85`, `sys.stdin.read()`). Under C.UTF-8 Python uses `surrogateescape`, so `printf '2024-03-01 food -5 caf\xe9\n' | pennywise list -` exits 0 and prints the raw byte, and `--json` emits a lone surrogate `"caf\udce9"`. The same bytes from a file exit 2. Under a non-UTF-8 locale stdin would be decoded with that locale's encoding. PRD: "Files are read as UTF-8", and a decode error should exit 2.
- **[IO-4]** `str.splitlines()` (`ledger.py:75`, as the PRD prescribes) treats FF, VT, U+001C–U+001E, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 as line breaks. A note containing one of them is cut short, the remainder becomes a phantom line, and reported line numbers no longer match physical lines. This contradicts the brief ("note is the rest of the line exactly as I wrote it", physical line numbers). The brief outranks the PRD here. Repro: `printf '2024-03-01 food -5 a\x0cb\n' > x; pennywise list x` gives `line 2: ...`.
- **[IO-5]** A UTF-8 BOM breaks line 1, for files and stdin. Repro: `printf '\xef\xbb\xbf2024-03-01 food -5\n' | pennywise list -` gives exit 1, `invalid date '\ufeff2024-03-01'`. `utf-8-sig` decoding would fix it.
- **[IO-6]** Cosmetic: `add` to a CRLF file appends an LF-terminated line, leaving mixed line endings (`cli.py:181`).
- **[IO-7]** Cosmetic: for unrecognized trailing arguments (`pennywise balance s.txt extra`, `add ... "-note"`) the error shows the top-level usage line `usage: pennywise [-h] COMMAND ...` instead of the subcommand's.
- **[OTHER-1]** Huge amounts crash. `format_amount`'s `quantize` (`ledger.py:133`) raises `decimal.InvalidOperation` under the default 28-digit precision. Repro: `printf '2024-03-01 a 999999999999999999999999999\n' > h; pennywise balance h` gives a traceback and exit 1; `list`, `summary`, `export` and `add` do the same (`add` writes nothing). Separately, `pennywise.balance` silently loses cents beyond 28 significant digits: `1000000000000000000000000000 + 0.01` returns `1000000000000000000000000000`. These amounts are far beyond household use, but the result is a traceback rather than a clean error.
- **[OTHER-2]** The brief's example output `1457.50` is arithmetically wrong; the code's `1557.50` is correct. Nothing to fix in the code. Mention it if anyone compares output against the brief literally.
